module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Mathoverflow 1973

Does the 6-sphere $S^6$ admit the structure of a complex manifold?

*References:*
- [mathoverflow/1973](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/1973/),
  asked by user [*Fetchinson0234*](https://mathoverflow.net/users/41312/victor-ramos).
- [Al26] L. Alpöge, [*A compact complex threefold fibred by tori over the projective line, and the six-sphere*](https://alpo.ge/s6.pdf) (2026),
  originally [shared on X](https://x.com/__alpoge__/status/2091639597193368014).
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped Manifold
namespace Mathoverflow1973

/-- The unit `n`-sphere, defined as `Metric.sphere 0 1` in `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n + 1))`. -/
abbrev unitSphere (n : ℕ) : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (n + 1))) := Metric.sphere 0 1

/--
Does the 6-sphere admit a complex structure, i.e. an atlas of holomorphically compatible charts
relating it to `EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)`? This is known as the Hopf Problem.

The answer is yes, see [Al26].
Formalisation of the proof by Boris Alexeev.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 32,
  formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/HopfProblem/blob/9ac8a456b526527837d7082ff775213ca8bc9809/Solution.lean"]
theorem mathoverflow_1973 :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ atlas : ChartedSpace (EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)) (unitSphere 6),
      IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ, EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)) 1 (unitSphere 6) := by
  sorry

end Mathoverflow1973

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement asks for a holomorphic atlas on the topological space S^6: `Metric.sphere 0 1` in ℝ^7 with the subspace topology, charts being `OpenPartialHomeomorph`s to ℂ^3. It does not require the complex structure to be compatible with the standard smooth structure of S^6, which is how the Hopf problem is usually read (a complex manifold diffeomorphic to S^6).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (Source ⇒ Lean) A complex structure on smooth S^6 is a holomorphic atlas (by Newlander–Nirenberg if it is given as an integrable J). Its charts are homeomorphisms between open subsets of S^6 and of ℂ^3, which gives a `ChartedSpace` whose transitions are holomorphic, hence `ContDiffOn ℂ 1`. (Lean ⇒ Source) Such an atlas makes S^6 a compact complex 3-fold X that is homeomorphic to S^6. So the underlying smooth manifold of X is a smooth homotopy 6-sphere. Θ_6 = 0 (Kervaire–Milnor) together with the h-cobordism theorem makes it diffeomorphic to standard S^6. Transporting the atlas along that diffeomorphism gives a complex structure compatible with the standard smooth structure. The source uses this route itself: Alpöge's Cor. 1.1 transports along a diffeomorphism X → S^6, Engel's Thm 4.1 goes Smale (topological) → Θ_6 = 0 (smooth), and Alpöge on X says "there aren't any exotic spheres in six dimensions". The linked Lean proof builds only a homeomorphism X ≃ₜ S^6 and transports the atlas, which is all the Lean statement needs.

reformulations.difference: The regularity is `IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ, EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)) 1`, i.e. transition maps that are `ContDiffOn ℂ 1`. A reader might take this as a real C^1 condition rather than holomorphic compatibility.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The model is `modelWithCornersSelf ℂ (EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3))`, so the condition is ℂ-C^1 on the open overlaps. I checked in Lean that it gives `DifferentiableOn ℂ` (holomorphic) transition maps. Conversely, holomorphic maps on open subsets of ℂ^3 are analytic, hence ℂ-C^∞ (Osgood/Cauchy on polydiscs; standard, but Mathlib has it only in one variable). So an `IsManifold … 1` atlas is exactly a holomorphic atlas. The linked proof builds an `ω` atlas and derives the `1` version with `infer_instance`.

sources_consulted: Mathlib source: Geometry/Manifold (ChartedSpace, IsManifold, contDiffGroupoid), Analysis/Complex/CauchyIntegral.lean
review.notes:
Status and formal_proof check. `@[category research solved]`, `answer(True)` and `formal_proof using lean4` agree with what MO 1973 records today. Robin Houston's community-wiki answer 514604 (2026-08-23) reports Alpöge's claimed positive solution, Boris Alexeev's Lean formalization (2026-08-27) and Philip Engel's 20-page exposition.

I fetched the linked Solution.lean at commit 9ac8a456… Its final theorem `Mathoverflow1973.mathoverflow_1973 : ∃ atlas : ChartedSpace (EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)) (unitSphere 6), letI := atlas; IsManifold 𝓘(ℂ, EuclideanSpace ℂ (Fin 3)) 1 (unitSphere 6)` is the repository's right-hand side. The repo's Challenge.lean has the same statement, and its Comparator config permits only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

I compiled the file in the sandbox with `lake env lean -DmaxHeartbeats=0`, using Lean v4.33.1 and the FC Mathlib; the proof targets v4.33.0. It finished in 816 s with exit 0 and no errors. `#print axioms` gives [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. An appended `example : (True ↔ ∃ atlas …, IsManifold … 1 (unitSphere 6)) := ⟨fun _ => mathoverflow_1973, fun _ => trivial⟩` type-checked. The file contains no sorry, axiom, opaque or native_decide. None of its 154 global instances gives a TopologicalSpace or ChartedSpace on the sphere; the instances that mention the sphere are Nonempty, Infinite, PathConnected, SimplyConnected and ContractibleSpace of a point-complement. I did not run the repo's lean4export/nanoda Comparator pipeline. Setting heartbeats to 0 only lifts resource limits and does not affect soundness.

Context. The informal construction has a holomorphic map to P^1, so a(X) = 1. This contradicts Campana–Demailly–Peternell (CDP98/CDP20), which says a complex S^6 has a(X) = 0, and MO comments raise that doubt. The paper's §10 argues that CDP's proofs are faulty. That dispute does not affect the formal statement, which asserts only the existence of a complex atlas, and the kernel-checked proof settles it.

In the repository environment I also confirmed that the bound `atlas` is the instance `IsManifold` uses (pp.explicit), that 𝕜 = ℂ, and that the sphere has the subspace topology. No degenerate atlas can exist: every point lies in the source of an open chart, and S^6 is compact, so it is not a single chart.

On the citation: Engel cites the manuscript as \"Claude and L. Alpöge\", using the PDF's first-page headline as the title. The file's \"[Al26] L. Alpöge, A compact complex threefold fibred by tori over the projective line, and the six-sphere\" uses the paper's actual title, which is acceptable.
